title: Understanding beginners’ mistakes with Haskell
authors: Ville Tirronen, Samuel Uusi-Mäkelä, Ville Isomöttönen
design: Eight-week elective; automatic error classification plus instructor/assistant manual session coding.
population: Mostly second–fourth-year university students with prior introductory programming.
findings: CouldntMatch occurred for 53/55 students. Of sessions with that error, 69% involved type confusion and roughly 30% precedence; one-third of type-confusion sessions came from one deliberately type-focused task. Missing recursive cases occurred, but authors did not observe the specific base-case-as-stopping-condition misconception. They reported no conceptual partial-application difficulty and little early laziness difficulty; syntax remained problematic.
limitations: Single cohort; coding infers intent from submissions; outside help and exploratory incomplete code possible; task exposure changes over time; no causal instructional comparison.

title: Investigating Compilation Errors of Students Learning Haskell
authors: Boldizsár Németh, Eunjong Choi, Erina Makihara, Hajimu Iida
design: Submission logs, nine teaching weeks; sampled manual root-cause classification and response/correction times.
population: First-year ELTE undergraduates; basic imperative experience in a statically typed language.
findings: Among sampled type-related errors: list/scalar/dimensional mismatch 20%; missing argument 8.6%; simple type mismatch 8.6%; wrong operation 8.4%; grouping/precedence 6.7%. Type errors predominated after initial weeks and were slower to repair. Some syntax mistakes produced misleading name/type diagnostics.
limitations: Error proportions are not learner prevalence. Anonymous sessions cannot track individuals across semester; instructor coding may misclassify intent; one curriculum. Only eventually fixed errors enter correction-time analysis.

title: Functional Baby Talk: Analysis of Code Fragments from Novice Haskell Programmers
design: Logs; expressions reparsed; sessions inferred by IP and ten-minute gaps.
population: 2016 Glasgow/FutureLearn MOOC users; prior background heterogeneous, not individually verified.
findings: Observed parenthesis, let/where, do-block binding/final-expression and range-notation errors. Unsupported data/type/multiline definitions were also attempted. About 100K inputs copied tutorial code versus 60K original, demonstrating why activity counts alone are weak learning measures.
limitations: One course, IP proxy and browser/OS selection; tool rejects some valid Haskell. Parsing failures do not establish a stable conceptual misconception or prevalence among unique learners.

title: Helium, for Learning Haskell
authors: Bastiaan Heeren, Daan Leijen, Arjan van IJzendoorn
design: Compiler/tool experience report and seven-week compilation logs.
population: University introductory functional-programming courses; exact student count not extracted.
findings: 31.6% of compilation attempts produced type errors; 46.3% were accepted. Undefined names dominated other static errors. Tool supplies source-oriented diagnostics and heuristics for swapped/missing arguments and related-function confusion.
limitations: Compiler acceptance is not task correctness or learning. Course/tasks and subset affect frequencies. Positive instructor/student feedback has no controlled learning comparison; undefined names include typos, so they do not establish scope misconceptions.

title: How Type Errors Were Fixed and What Students Did?
design: Retrospective program-sequence and repair analysis; manually identified intended fixes.
population: Three university Haskell cohorts (2002,2003,2017), including first-year learners.
findings: Over 45% of final type-error fixes in each dataset added/removed parentheses or brackets. Wrong annotations appeared in 28%,34.4%,27% of analyzed errors. Actual fixes often differ from the location suggested by diagnostics. Type signatures may be initially wrong or become stale after definition changes.
limitations: Not every original ill-typed program analyzed: 1000 sampled of 2000 in first dataset. Approximately 6% lacked usable reference repair and were excluded. Repair sequences support behavior, not direct mental-model diagnoses. Cohort/task/compiler differences.

title: Structural versus Pipeline Composition of Higher-Order Functions (Experience Report)
design: Seven input-output planning problems; same operator pairs structural/pipeline; partly randomized order; five-day response window.
population: Accelerated introductory CS students after higher-order-function reading/assignment.
findings: Apparently correct narrative structural compositions:37,31,31; pipeline:22,10 for first two problems. Third pipeline problem admitted an unintended simpler solution. Some students treated map as fold, confused filter/take-while, or could not infer intermediate transformations.
limitations: Small single-institution task study; no Haskell/static-checker test. Input-output ambiguity, first structural question fixed, nonmandatory surveillance, and unintended solutions limit generalization. Difficulty comparison is task-specific; pedagogic sequencing remains a hypothesis.

title: Plan Composition Using Higher-Order Functions
authors: Elijah Rivera, Shriram Krishnamurthi, Robert Goldstone
design: HOF recognition, behavioral explanations, planning then programming; month-long placement module.
population: Selective US university placement/accelerated CS module; ~90% prior computing, nearly all new to FP.
findings: Only 10/402 plans were explicitly wrong; most implementations passed instructor tests. Composition-recognition errors often omitted an outer map, treating nested inputs as flattened examples. Understanding single HOFs did not imply identical performance across representations.
limitations: No control group or retention/transfer test; high selectivity/prior experience; ceiling effects; author coding and tool affordances affect interpretation. Plan success does not prove planning intervention caused learning.

title: Empirical studies of functional programming learners evaluating recursive functions
design: Empirical recursive-function evaluation studies; details unverified.
population: Students; exact level/prior knowledge unverified.
findings: Publisher abstract confirms observations of misconceptions and processing strategies while learners evaluated Miranda recursion. Specific categories, denominators and teaching-effect claims cannot be independently extracted from this abstract.
limitations: Full text unavailable in this track; Haskell transfer is indirect. Tirronen2015 reports non-observation of a recursion misconception attributed to this paper.

title: The Dys-functional student
design: Teaching experience/mistake catalogue; exact empirical design unverified.
findings: Abstract describes observed student mistakes in language features, program concepts and imperative-paradigm legacy, with proposed remedies. Do not infer prevalence, causal negative transfer, or exact misconceptions from abstract.
limitations: 1995 original copyright/conference year; 2005 online release is not original study year. Author page mentions a PDF but exposed no downloadable link in inspected text; publisher preview only.

title: Obstacles when teaching functional programming
limitations: Exact-title searches and DOI access did not provide primary full text. No misconception or outcome claims extracted.

title: Goanna: a novel approach for automated type error debugging
authors: Shuai Fu, Tim Dwyer, Peter J. Stuckey, John C. Grundy
design: Corpus diagnostic accuracy and generated performance benchmarks; no completed rigorous learner experiment.
population: Historical Helium student-program corpus; current learner study planned.
findings: Reports diagnostic accuracy 81.6% Goanna versus 65.5% Helium and 33.7% GHC. Preliminary workshop reactions were positive; rigorous human evaluation is future work.
limitations: Accuracy is a tool-performance outcome, not evidence of conceptual learning, retention, transfer or debugging independence. Historical corpus, supported-language subset, and computational cost constrain applicability.

title: GeckoGraph: A visual language for polymorphic types
authors: Shuai Fu, Tim Dwyer, Peter J. Stuckey, John C. Grundy
design: Preregistered ten-task gamified experiment; counterbalanced groups alternate graphical/text notation at odd/even levels.
population: Haskell Reddit/Discord volunteers; self-rated expertise, not a classroom sample.
findings: No overall significant time/success advantage. Beginner aggregate success95.12% versus92.68%,p=.0431. Task10 beginner success94.9% versus80.4%,p=.0452:14.5 percentage points. Familiar task10 difference11.2points has p=.136.
limitations: Reported N contradicts subgroup totals; Shapiro-Wilk interpretation is reversed; familiar task10 rejection claim contradicts p=.136. Repeated-task dependence/multiple comparisons require scrutiny. Artificial tasks, skips, self-selection, ceiling effects; performance with aid is not retained learning.

title: Teaching computer programming with PRIMM: a sociocultural perspective
authors: Sue Sentance, Jane Waite, Maria Kallia
access: selected full-text sections of 42-page manuscript: participant recruitment, assessments, results and limitations
design: mixed-methods classroom comparison; volunteer teachers trained in PRIMM; usual school materials in controls; 8–12 weeks
population: English secondary-school pupils aged 11–14 learning Python
findings: PRIMM group had higher post-test scores; reported rank-test effect r=.13. Teacher interviews described practical benefits.
limitations: Author-stated: volunteer teachers, insufficient demographic data, nonvalidated assessments, uncontrolled comparator lessons. Reviewer: teacher training/materials/dialogue form a bundle; no randomized Haskell or self-paced university test. Do not repeat the manuscript's interpretation of r=.13 as 13% variance explained.

title: Reducing withdrawal and failure rates in introductory programming with subgoal labeled worked examples
authors: Lauren E. Margulieux, Briana B. Morrison, Adrienne Decker
access: selected publisher full-text sections: Method, Participants, quiz/exam results
design: semester classroom quasi-experiment comparing conventional versus subgoal-labeled worked examples
population: university introductory Java students; five course sections
findings: Better formative quiz performance, but no statistically significant improvement in average exam performance; lower exam variance and fewer withdrawals/failing exam averages reported.
limitations: Section/instructor effects and selection remain possible; one control section online. Outcomes vary by measure. Earlier 2019 design and explanation-response papers reuse this project and are not independent replications.

title: From Studying Examples to Solving Problems: Fading Worked-Out Solution Steps Helps Learning
authors: Alexander Renkl, Robert K. Atkinson, Uwe H. Maier
access: selected full-text sections of six-page Cognitive Science Society proceedings paper
design: classroom quasi-experiment; randomized laboratory fading versus example/problem pairs
population: German ninth-grade physics classes; Mississippi State psychology students learning probability
findings: Fading benefited near-transfer performance in both studies; neither showed a significant far-transfer benefit.
limitations: Small samples and immediate domain-specific assessments; different fading directions across studies. Haskell benefit is inferred. Distinct from Renkl/Atkinson 2003 conceptual paper.

title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
authors: Henry L. Roediger III, Jeffrey D. Karpicke
access: selected full-text Methods, Results and General Discussion; author-lab PDF
design: two experiments: prose study/re-study versus free recall without feedback; immediate and delayed tests
population: Washington University undergraduates aged 18–24
findings: Restudy favored five-minute performance; retrieval favored delayed retention. Experiment 2: repeated-testing group recalled 61% versus repeated-study 40% after one week.
limitations: Prose idea-unit recall, not programming construction or type inference. Retrieval and study periods differed in duration; avoid claiming identical practice time in every condition. Not evidence that reading is dispensable.

title: Spacing Effects in Learning: A Temporal Ridgeline of Optimal Retention
authors: Nicholas J. Cepeda, Edward Vul, Doug Rohrer, John T. Wixted, Harold Pashler
access: selected full-text current-study, Methods, Discussion; university-hosted published PDF
design: random assignment to 26 gap/retention-interval combinations; 32 trivia facts; recall and recognition
population: online adult memory panel; ages 18–72, mean 34
findings: Optimal review gap depended on retention interval; performance rose then fell with increasing gap. Approximate optimal ratios: 20–40% for one-week delay, 5–10% for one-year delay.
limitations: Trivia retention and completer analysis; attrition increased at longer delays. Not a universal 10–20% schedule or demonstrated programming retention effect.

title: Enhancing Syntax Error Messages Appears Ineffectual
authors: Paul Denny, Andrew Luxton-Reilly, Dave Carpenter
access: selected full-text Evaluation, Results and Discussion; university-hosted PDF
design: random allocation; 10 short CodeWrite method-body exercises over weeks 2–3; raw versus enhanced syntax messages
population: University of Auckland accelerated summer CS1 students learning Java
findings: No significant benefit on consecutive noncompiling submissions, overall noncompiling attempts, or correction attempts for common error categories.
limitations: Single short course, small tasks and specific enhancement style; no delayed conceptual assessment. Null result does not establish all enhancements ineffective.

title: Effective compiler error message enhancement for novice programming students
authors: Brett A. Becker, Graham Glanville, Ricardo Iwashima, Claire McDonnell, Kyle Goslin, Catherine Mooney
access: selected full-text author-uploaded original manuscript on ResearchGate; author-site accepted PDF redirected to suspended page
design: successive-year control/intervention comparison; Decaf raw versus raw plus enhanced messages
population: first-semester Java CS1 students at one Irish institution
findings: Reduced error-frequency and several repeated-error measures under enhancement.
limitations: Historical cohorts, no random allocation; compiler IDs approximate students, some duplication/other-tool use possible. Error frequency is not independent mastery. Similar error-rank distributions across languages do not prove equivalent instructional effects.

title: Not the Silver Bullet: LLM-enhanced Programming Error Messages are Ineffective in Practice
authors: Eddie Antonio Santos, Brett A. Becker
access: selected author full-text HTML: participants, procedure, results and limitations
design: within-participant six-task debugging study; task-specific random assignment to GCC, handwritten or GPT-4 explanations
population: European university first-year CS students, second programming semester, C
findings: GPT-4 was faster than stock messages on only one task; handwritten explanations generally performed better. Preference for GPT-4 did not imply faster repair.
limitations: Six selected bugs, timed repair, permitted web search; same researcher authored bugs and expert messages; GPT-4 also displayed stock messages. No delayed learning measure. Findings cannot establish current-model or Haskell effectiveness.

title: Understanding Conceptual Transfer for Students Learning New Programming Languages
access: selected author-uploaded full-text sections: participants, study procedures and results; institutional record has abstract only
design: two within-participant paper-based code-comprehension studies; categories of true, false and abstract true carryover
population: near-novice undergraduates Python→Java; IT masters students Java→Python
findings: Syntax similarity accompanied positive or negative semantic transfer depending on whether meaning carried over; dissimilar syntax impeded recognition of shared concepts.
limitations: Observational within-learner comparisons, selected concept categories and different test orders; not an intervention effect or imperative→Haskell result.

title: Notional Machines and Introductory Programming Education
access: selected author-uploaded full-text introduction and conceptual discussion; institutional metadata verified
design: narrative/conceptual review, not a new intervention experiment
findings: Proposes making the program-execution model an explicit learning objective and relates this to mental models and programming difficulties.
limitations: Framework evidence, not an effect estimate; no new N. A Haskell notional machine must respect non-strict evaluation rather than importing imperative state/line-order semantics.

title: Students’ ways of experiencing visual program simulation
authors: Juha Sorva, Jan Lönnberg, Lauri Malmi
access: abstract and institutional metadata only; attempted publisher full-text open failed
design: qualitative interviews plus supplementary observation
population: novice programmers; precise course/language not verified
findings: Six ways of experiencing simulation reported; some learners failed to attach meaning to visuals or connect them to programming practice.
limitations: Abstract-only extraction: no verified N, interview protocol, sampling or coding details. Evidence of differing interpretations, not a causal visualization benefit or prevalence estimate.

title: Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students
access: selected publisher full-text Methods, Results and Discussion
design: individual RCT rewarding practice days versus question counts; instructor-cluster RCT of same incentive
population: university introductory Python; high-school/college Java courses
findings: Day incentives increased practice days. Within-course exam gains particularly benefited lower-GPA students; second experiment measured practice behavior, not comparable learning outcomes.
limitations: Postrandomization exclusions, modeled GPA interaction; same adaptive/interleaving tool in both arms. Incentive effect is not pure spacing mediation causality; similar practice/assessment question types and one-course learning result limit transfer.

title: Map, Filter, and Conquer: A Visual Tool for Learning Higher-Order Functions
authors: Silvan Renggli, Sverrir Thorgeirsson, Theo B. Weidmann, Zhendong Su
design: Randomized order, within-subject crossover; two hours; two tutorials up to 45 minutes, four HOFs; first-attempt implementation, behavior questions and Paas effort.
findings: Reported effort 4.78 versus 6.04, d=1.03, p<.001; implementation errors 1.33 versus 2.89. Excluding Python syntax errors gives 1.70 and nonsignificant difference, p=.058. Behavioral questions also nonsignificant. Time 16.8 versus 25.6 minutes.
limitations: Brief intervention, carryover despite distractor, selected tasks, first-attempt scoring; procedural tool performance is not retention/transfer. Self-reported load; syntax protection confounds conceptual benefit.

title: Teaching types with a cognitively effective worked example format
design: Repeated single-subject A-B-A; textbook baseline, five worked derivations plus deduction rules, then baseline; early master-level FP course.
findings: Specific individuals confused application/abstraction, type-variable scope across signatures, currying and type classes. Beginner gains with derivations had mixed maintenance; advanced students had little scope to improve. Prototype analogy survey 9/18 yes, including explanations.
limitations: Exploratory volunteers, no general validation; repeated tasks and stricter intervention scoring, protocol deviations, extra individual correction, omitted hardest questions. Pilot versus volunteer accounting unclear; no long-term retention.

title: Developing Behavioral Concepts of Higher-Order Functions
design: Five optional clustering/classification stages; first four over month, fifth three months later; behavioral examples/diagrams.
findings: Filter/take-while distinctions remained harder than map/filter; fold's universality complicates classifications. Stage 5 persistence supports targeted behavioral probes. Authors recommend justifications and learner-generated examples; diagram superiority not established.
limitations: Changing samples; Stage 4 identities missing; no matched retention estimate or causal instruction comparison. Small HOF set, ambiguous examples, prior exposure, optional participation; recognition not coding or constructing function arguments.

title: Observations on the Design of Program Planning Notations for Students
authors: Elijah Rivera, Shriram Krishnamurthi, Kathi Fisler
design: Two consecutive novice-course offerings: Fall 2022 blocks and Spring 2023 free-form paper; work artifacts, optional feedback and interviews.
findings: Earlier experienced-student block-planning success did not carry over cleanly. Novices described rigid/time-consuming planning; many supplied code-like plans or completed plans after coding. Paper plans favored to-do lists; mechanisms for composing subtasks remained underspecified.
limitations: Experience report, cohort/task changes and self-selection; no causal learning comparison or complete Spring denominator. Interviews concern selected mixed-notation users; inspect expectations and practical benefit before imposing a planner.

title: Study on difficulties and misconceptions with modern type systems
design: Mirrored abstract describes multiple-choice items in online introductory FP course; primary methods unavailable.
limitations: ACM DOI inaccessible; ResearchGate says no full text; OpenAlex no OA location. Primary sample, language, items and coding unverified.

title: Evaluating the Tracing of Recursion in the Substitution Notional Machine
authors: Preston Tunnell Wilson, Kathi Fisler, Shriram Krishnamurthi
design: Single-course repeated diagnostic quizzes, followed by language/model transition
population: Introductory summer course, no prerequisites

title: Teaching the Art of Functional Programming using Automated Grading (Experience Report)
design: Course experience and grader extension design
population: Second-year programming languages course, Fall 2018

title: Stepping OCaml
authors: Tsukino Furukawa, Youyou Cong, Kenichi Asai
design: Three annual cohorts with changing tool support and instruction
population: Second-year CS, prior C course

title: Haskelite: A Tracing Interpreter Based on a Pattern-Matching Calculus
design: Operational semantics and interpreter design

title: An Interactive Learning Environment for Program Design
authors: Kouta Kumamoto, Youyou Cong, Hidehiko Masuhara
design: One-task user study with logs, generated code and questionnaire
population: Undergraduate introductory FP course; atomic and nonrecursive algebraic data covered

title: Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback
authors: Alex Gerdes, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, L. Thomas van Binsbergen
design: Three technical/user evaluations; model-solution recognition and property-based feedback; no controlled learning comparison.
population: University Haskell learners; different course cohorts.
findings: Stepwise hints can address partial programs and counterexamples. The 2013 evaluation contains 1,920 compiler-error interactions (55.4% of diagnoses), but 142 of 652 attempts (21.8%) ended in compiler error. These are interaction/attempt denominators, not learner prevalence. Authors explicitly leave learning effects to future work.
limitations: Accuracy, coverage and perceived usefulness do not establish retention or transfer. Recognition depends on model solutions and supported strategies; alternative valid programs may be unrecognized.

title: Teaching Introductory Functional Programming Using Haskelite
design: Teaching experience, voluntary qualitative feedback and historical course results.
population: Porto first-year students, mostly prior Python; spring 2024.
findings: Learners reported usefulness for inspecting recursion and higher-order functions. Trace size and unsupported valid Haskell syntax created difficulties; the tool needs explicit subset messages. Distinguish the tool's six-response questionnaire from the separate institutional fifteen-response course survey.
limitations: Small self-selected feedback; course changes and historical pass rates cannot identify the tool's causal effect. Tool implements a Haskell subset. Short semantic traces are not an exact account of optimized GHC execution.

title: Evaluating Haskell expressions in a tutoring environment
authors: Tim Olmer, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring
design: Prototype and small formative usability survey.
population: Invited functional-programming teachers and students.
findings: The prototype diagnoses learner-entered rewrite steps under different evaluation strategies. Respondents differed over how much strategy choice and detail learners should see.
limitations: Feasibility and usability evidence; no controlled learning gains. Small response groups. Multiple strategies may overwhelm beginners, so a default strategy is an instructional choice to test.

title: Experiences of early assessment to teach functional programming
design: Historical-cohort comparison, online first-year course during COVID, 2021 versus 2022.
population: First-year discrete-mathematics/Haskell course; students completing both assessments.
findings: Adding an early summative Use-Modify assessment accompanied a later Create-assessment mean of 62.249 versus 53.256: 8.993 percentage points; one-tailed Wilcoxon p=.0371, reported r=.164. Both cohorts already used formative Use-Modify-Create.
limitations: Small reported effect, nonrandom cohorts, completer selection, changed recordings and other context; mathematics means decreased. Association cannot establish causality or delayed transfer.

title: Learner experiences of a blended course incorporating a MOOC on Haskell functional programming
authors: Vicki H. M. Dale, Jeremy Singer
design: Survey and focus group in blended honours course; no randomized comparator.
population: Fourth-year Glasgow students, 2016–17; first six of ten weeks used a MOOC.
findings: Respondents valued flexibility and learning activities but reported poorly signposted support and discontinuity into more advanced work. Integration of help and progression warrants design attention.
limitations: Self-selected perceptions, not demonstrated learning effects. One advanced university course; cannot rank MOOCs against classroom teaching.

title: Using Student-created Instructional Videos in CS Upper-level Courses: A Successful Strategy in a Functional Programming Course
design: Small uncontrolled pre/post classroom experience with two student-made explanatory videos.
population: Senior functional-programming course at Universidad El Bosque, Colombia; ages 18–35.
findings: Assessment improvement and positive perceptions accompanied students making concept/code explanation videos; participants also found production time-consuming.
limitations: No comparator; improvement can reflect normal course learning, practice or selection. Do not equate video production with a demonstrated causal self-explanation effect or transfer to beginner Haskell.

title: The risks and benefits of teaching purely functional programming in first year
authors: Manuel M. T. Chakravarty, Gabriele Keller
design: Teaching experience based on several large first-year classes and surveys; detail not independently extracted.
population: First-year classes, reportedly up to 600.
findings: Abstract frames functional programming as a means to teach problem solving and computer science rather than paradigm advocacy as an end.
limitations: Full text not inspected; no causal claim about benefits or harm, and no extracted effect size.
